notes.title: An Ode to Restraint: Lessons from the Tim Cook Legacy
notes.text: Market cap rose from $1.68 billion at the start of Jobs's tenure to over $4 trillion at end-2025; Cook added $3.64 trillion. Jobs-era price appreciation 47.19% a year compounded (1997-2011). Revenue grew 23.67% a year under Jobs and 8.52% (2012-2025) under Cook, with nearly $800 billion of buybacks, dividends since 2012 and a $17 billion debt issue in 2013; net debt always negative. Its share of Mag Seven capex fell from 8.04% to 3.02%. He calls it a mature, cash-returning, cautious business and says he has been a shareholder through much of both tenures.

notes.title: Apple and Amazon at a Trillion $: Looking Back and Looking Forward!
notes.text: Value $200 vs price $219 (Sept 18, 2018): overvalued by about 9%. "Predominately a smart phone company" with about 62% of revenue from the iPhone, a maturing and competitive business; operating margin falls from 30% to about 25% over five years. 2014-2018: returned $277 billion ($61 billion dividends, $216 billion buybacks) vs $242 billion of free cash flow to equity. Leaned toward selling.

notes.title: Trillion Dollar Toppers: Market Triggers, Value Drivers and Pricing Catalysts!
notes.text: Triggers like a trillion-dollar market cap are unlikely to change value, though they may draw attention; he owns Apple shares.

notes.title: Apple: The Greatest Cash Machine in History?
notes.text: Held Apple 2010-2012, sold in April 2012, bought again in 2015 below his estimate and held through the rally. Earlier values: about $130 in Aug 2015 (price $110) and about $126 in Feb 2016 ($94). Slow revenue growth, margins declining with smartphone competition, possible larger tax bill on trapped cash. Sell trigger set at $140 a share, the top of his value range.

notes.title: Fairness Opinions: Fix them or Flush them!
notes.text: Illustrative valuation from his May 2016 analysis: values range from $80.81 to $415.63, and a $160 price sits at about the 92nd percentile: "possible, but neither plausible, nor probable." Used to argue for reforming fairness opinions.

notes.title: Icahn exits, Buffett enters, Whither Apple? Value and Price Effects of Big Name Investing
notes.text: Carl Icahn sold his entire stake (Apr 28, 2016); his 2015 letter argued $240 a share (2016 EPS $12 at P/E 18 plus $24.44 of cash per share), which Damodaran calls "casual pricing," not intrinsic value. Berkshire Hathaway (Combs and Weschler) took a new stake (May 16, 2016). He agrees Apple is a mature company whose cash flows can cover dividends. Prior post put the price at about $93.

notes.title: DCF Myth 3.2: If you don't look, its not there!
notes.text: Monte Carlo valuation: $126.47 base case vs about $93 (under a 10% probability the stock is worth less than $93). Revenue growth cut to 1.50% (from 2.2% in his Feb 2016 valuation of $129.80), margin centered on 25%, growth-margin correlation 0.50, cash of about $232 billion net of an expected $28 billion tax liability. Is again an Apple shareholder after selling in summer 2015.

notes.title: Race to the top: The Duel between Alphabet and Apple!
notes.text: Value $126 vs $94 price: undervalued by about 25%. Prefers Apple as an investment; sees Alphabet as the better business and momentum trade.

notes.title: A Violent Earnings Season: Pricing and Value Perspectives
notes.text: Used as a price-versus-value example in a post on earnings season; no new valuation.

notes.title: Narrative Resets: Revisiting a Tech Trio (Apple, Facebook and Twitter)
notes.text: Value about $130 a share vs a price under $110 (down from $128 in March). Mature company with revenue growth under 5%, margin pressure offset by strong iPhone 6 margins, a small chance of another disruptive product; Apple Pay a possible breakthrough. Waiting a few weeks before buying; expects to be a shareholder again.

notes.title: Reacting to Earnings Reports: Let's get real!
notes.text: Value $96.55/share; plans to exit if price reaches $100, otherwise holds.

notes.title: Watch the Gap: Apple's long and twisted pricing journey
notes.text: Value $648-675 a share (his table lists $674 on Apr 24; later $675 after a share-count correction to 861.38 million) vs $525 before earnings and $594 at the post: about 12% below value. Revenue growth about 5% with margin pressure; buybacks and dividends do not change operating asset value; the 7-for-1 split is cosmetic; a further $17 billion bond issue adds about $5 a share. "I will continue to hold Apple but I have learned to remain vigilant."

notes.title: The Brand Name Advantage: Valuable, Sustainable and Elusive
notes.text: Cites Interbrand's $98.3 billion brand value; says Apple's price premium is only partly brand (software, features and quality matter too).

notes.title: Rebirth and Reincarnation: Escaping the corporate death spiral
notes.text: Valued at $600 a share; a good investment but he does not yet see the ingredients for rebirth, so he waits.

notes.title: Apple: News, Noise and Value
notes.text: Value about $588 vs $420 on Apr 28, 2013, after lowering revenue growth and target margins and adding debt; the price already implies low growth and declining margins. Hold.

notes.title: Hundred dollar bills are hard to come by!
notes.text: Argues Apple's cash cannot be unlocked easily and criticizes Cook's communication with investors.

notes.title: Financial Alchemy: David Einhorn's "value" play for Apple
notes.text: Einhorn's preferred-stock proposal creates no value, though it might act as a price catalyst.

notes.title: Back to Apple: Thoughts on value, price and the confidence gap
notes.text: Value $608 vs $440 (about 90% chance undervalued); a large value-price gap may not close quickly because of the confidence gap. Holds it, capped at 10% of his portfolio.

notes.title: Market Mayhem: Lessons for Apple
notes.text: Advice to Apple after the market mayhem: rebuild investor trust, be more transparent, choose a growth or mature identity and act on it, pursue disruption in new markets.

notes.title: Are you a value investor? Take the Apple test
notes.text: Value $609 a share vs $440 (about 38% upside). Buy for value investors who pass the gut and confidence checks; he bought at $500 and does not plan to add.

notes.title: Apple's Crown Jewel: Valuing the iPhone Franchise
notes.text: Values the iPhone franchise at about $307 billion using a product life-cycle model (margins, two-year upgrade cycle, customer switching), roughly half of the $623.5 billion market value reached on Aug 20. No explicit call; he sold in April 2012.

notes.title: Earnings surprises, price reaction and value
notes.text: Earnings-surprise post: a pre-report valuation spreadsheet is linked; no value stated; readers judge how the report affects their strategy. He sold his shares in April 2012.

stocks.summary: Damodaran's most-covered stock, and the one he trades most. He valued it undervalued in 2013 and 2015-16 (about $126-130 vs prices in the $90s-$110s) and overvalued in 2018 ($200 vs $219) and again in 2020, selling each time the price ran ahead; by 2024 he had it about 6% overvalued ($176.79 vs $188). He treats it as a mature smartphone company where brand, ecosystem and services are hard to separate, argues a trillion-dollar market cap or stock split changes nothing about value, and in 2026 reviews Jobs vs Cook era value creation.

notes.title: The Greed & Fear Tango: The Markets in April 2025!
notes.text: Fell about 10% in the first two days of April then recovered to within 1% of the start-of-month level; implied ERP 4.59% to 4.58% after rising above 5%. VIX peaked at 52.33 on April 8 and ended at 24.70. Mag Seven down $2.6T year to date; he holds six of the seven.

notes.title: Anatomy of a Market Crisis: Tariffs, Markets and the Economy!
notes.text: US equities lost $5.3 trillion in the week (down 9.24% from March 28). Implied ERP rose from 4.57% on April 2 to 5.08%. Compares with 2008 (equities fell 28% from Sept 12 to Dec 31, ERP near 8%) and 2020 (down 33%, ERP 7.75%).

notes.title: Data Update 3 for 2025: The times they are a'changin'!
notes.text: Mag Seven added $5.6 trillion in 2024, nearly all of the market's gain, and $15.8 trillion over 2014-2024 (about 40% of the increase). Technology added $4.63 trillion in 2024. He argues the small-cap premium is not returning; large caps beat small caps by about 4-4.5% a year over 20 years; low price-to-book stocks have trailed by 0.87% a year since about 1990.

stocks.summary: The market-level posts, mostly his monthly and annual updates. He computes the implied equity risk premium (about 4.0-4.6% through 2025-26, 4.42% in July 2026) and a fair-value index level, which has run from mildly overvalued to about 12% overvalued, and repeats that he does not time the market and that backtests of CAPE-based timing rules add nothing. Recent themes: Mag Seven concentration, buybacks ($1.153 trillion in 2025), the April 2025 tariff drop, the March 2026 Iran-war rise in risk premium, and the Nov 5, 2026 AI selloff that cut about $1.8 trillion in a day.

notes.title: META Lesson 3: Tell me a story!
notes.text: Feb 2022 valuation $346 a share vs $220 then; price just over $100 at the post. "Doomsday" scenario (advertising income frozen at trailing level, 20-year life, no liquidation value, R&D about $32 billion a year, Metaverse losses of $10 billion a year with no payoff, cost of capital 9%) gives equity value $258.6 billion, or $330 billion excluding the Metaverse, so Metaverse spending costs about $71 billion. Market cap $247 billion on Oct 29 and $311 billion on Nov 15 (implied Metaverse value destruction about $18.9 billion). Bought at $133 after the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal and kept it; doubled his holding on Nov 4, 2022, an exception to his rule against doubling down. Admits he has no influence on management. notes.title: The IPO of the decade? My valuation of Facebook
notes.text: Pre-IPO Facebook: base-case equity value about $71.6 billion (about $29.05 a share; Class A about $28), simulation median about $70 billion, 10% chance above $117 billion and 10% at or below $43 billion, vs a preliminary IPO range of $75-100 billion. Assumes 40% compound revenue growth for five years fading to the 2.01% risk-free rate by year 10, pre-tax margin from above 45% down to 35%, $1.50 of revenue per $1 of new capital, cost of capital 11.42% falling to 8%. Would not buy at $75 billion: the price assumes near-superlative success and the dual-class structure gives holders no say. "Could it be worth $100 billion? Sure, but you are fighting the odds as an investor."

stocks.summary: He valued pre-IPO Facebook at about $29 a share and called the $38 IPO a 'long-term sell', then bought at $18 after it fell. Later valuations: overvalued in 2013 ($27.65 vs $38), about fair in 2016, $181 vs $155 in 2018 (undervalued), the most undervalued FANGAM stock in 2020-22, and about fairly valued in 2024 ($445 vs $456). In 2022 he used Meta as a lessons series on governance, accounting for R&D and the metaverse; in 2025-26 he criticizes its metaverse spend, Blue Owl data-center financing and Zuckerberg's voting control, but says he holds it.

notes.title: Tesla in November 2023 : Story twists and turns, with value consequences!
notes.text: Value about $180 a share from a business-by-business breakdown (auto, energy, software, robotaxi); his January 2023 median was $153. Price below $200 (he cites $197): overvalued "at least based on my story." Trailing revenue $95.9 billion, operating income $10.7 billion (11.18% margin); auto gross margin 17.42% in Q3; energy 6.2% of revenue; Model 3 cut by $1,250 to about $39,000; FSD priced at $12,000 and still in beta; Cybertruck reservations over two million but he expects sales to fall short. notes.title: Disagreements and First Principles: The Pushback on my Tesla Valuation
notes.text: Value about $130 a share, "overvalued, albeit only mildly." notes.title: Tesla's Trillion Dollar Moment: A Valuation Revisit!
notes.text: Value per share $571 in his most upbeat scenario, less than half the market price: overvalued, and he would not invest; sold his shares in January 2020 and does not short because "momentum beats fundamentals" in the short term. Assumes revenue about $414 billion by 2032 (roughly ten million cars plus ancillary), a 16% operating margin, sales-to-capital 4.00, cost of capital 6% (risk-free 1.56%, ERP 4.62%), no failure risk; equity value about $692 billion ($640 billion for common). He admits he has repeatedly underestimated Tesla's value and calls it a "trade," not an "investment." Market cap rose from $2.8 billion (Aug 2010) to over $1 trillion.

Calls the SolarCity acquisition an "unforced error."

notes.title: Twists and Turns in the Tesla Story : A Boring, Boneheaded Update!
notes.text: Revalued at about $186 a share vs a price of about $340; his optimistic "Royal Flush" scenario gives about $412. Story: revenue up tenfold to about $120 billion, pre-tax margin 12%, sales-to-capital about 2.25, cost of capital 8.29%, $14 billion of new capital in the royal flush case ($22 billion in his base case, with cash flows negative for eight years); production of about 30,000 cars a week by year 10. Debt is a survival risk for the next year or two. No explicit trade call, but "if you are bullish, that should scare you." Calls the 2016 SolarCity deal "ill-advised"; BMW (9.89% margin) is the benchmark.

He bought in 2019 near fair value, sold in January 2020 at $640, and exited fully by May 2025 after selling in the tariff selloff. He never shorted, citing momentum, argues Musk is a net positive to value, and in Dec 2025 shows Tesla needs 86% five-year revenue growth to justify its market cap.

A value above $400 is possible but unlikely; the price is "pushing towards the 95th percentile" and breakeven needs extraordinary growth plus margins near 50%. Bought in 2018 after a drop of over 50% and sold half at these prices, keeping the rest for optionality. Flags dependence on TSMC and China-Taiwan risk.

Musk owns about 42% of equity and about 80% of the votes. At $1.25 trillion EV: about 80x sales and 156x EBITDA. Segment assumptions: launch market $30 billion growing to $100 billion by 2036, share falling from over 80% to 70%, margin 40%; Starlink internet market $15 billion to $160 billion, share 75%, margin near 60% (about 10,000 satellites and over 10 million subscribers at end-2025); xAI 2036 revenue $80 billion at a 50% margin; expansion options $50 billion of revenue at a 30% margin after 2032. Calls the 8% cost of capital reasonable because the risk is company-specific and two-sided.

profile: Aswath Damodaran is a Professor of Finance at NYU's Stern School of Business, where he has taught corporate finance and valuation since 1986. He holds an MBA and PhD from UCLA and is widely known as the 'Dean of Valuation'. He has won Stern's teaching award several times and was voted most popular business school professor in a 2011 Business Week poll.

He wrote the standard texts Investment Valuation, The Dark Side of Valuation and The Little Book of Valuation, along with Corporate Finance and Investment Fables, and posts his data sets, spreadsheets and class material free on his NYU site. Every January he updates data on country risk, margins, betas and the implied equity risk premium.

Musings on Markets, running since 2008, is where he applies this to live cases: Tesla, Apple, Uber, Nvidia and more recently SpaceX and Anthropic. His method is to tell a story about the business, convert it into revenue, margin and reinvestment assumptions, then compare the resulting value with the market price. He usually discloses whether he bought or sold, and he does not time the market.

profile: John Huber is the portfolio manager and managing member of Saber Capital Management, a value-focused firm in North Carolina that runs separate client accounts and a partnership modeled on Buffett's 1950s partnerships. The accounts have no lockups, and Saber manages nearly all of Huber's own investable capital and most of his family's net worth.

Base Hit Investing is his Substack, an extension of his personal investing journal, with tens of thousands of subscribers. It mixes stock write-ups with thinking on portfolio management, ROIC and behavior. Free posts cover some ideas; paid posts carry the full archive and company research. He says it is educational, not a recommendation service.

Approach: patient, long-term value investing in high-quality businesses bought below their worth, with a heavy focus on free cash flow yield, return on invested capital, buybacks and capital allocation. 'Saber' and 'Base Hit' are baseball metaphors from sabermetrics: get on base steadily rather than swing for home runs.

profile: Praetorian Capital Fund is a concentrated, long-biased hedge fund run by founder and CIO Harris Kupperman. It began investing on January 1, 2019 and writes quarterly letters to investors.

How it invests: a core book of a handful of concentrated, asymmetric positions (typically at least 5% of capital each, mostly companies worth $1-5 billion, never above 5% of a company), plus an Event-Driven book of shorter situations. Its themes are inflation and fiscal stress ('Project Zimbabwe'), a weaker US dollar and emerging markets, precious metals, uranium, offshore energy and refiners. It avoids large-cap tech and expects most AI capital to be impaired.

Fund facts from the letters: about $343 million of net assets at March 2024 and about $350 million with 198 investors at September 2024; a 1.25% management fee and a 20% incentive allocation; a Cayman offshore vehicle. Returns are unaudited estimates.
